title: A Call to Lagrangian Action: Learning Population Mechanics from Temporal Snapshots
claim: Second-order Lagrangian mechanics on populations capture momentum-driven dynamics that first-order gradient flows cannot, and they recover gradient flows when heavily damped.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, manifold sketch beside four-snapshot particle sequence
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a), on the left, shows a grey curved surface standing for the space of probability measures. A dotted grey path runs through black points p0 and p1, with an intermediate grey point p_Δt below the path. A red dashed loop leaves p0 and returns near it, and a purple dotted arrow continues from p1 to a purple point p_{1+Δt}. Panel (b), on the right, shows four square boxes in a row. Each box holds small blue arrow-shaped particles at p0, p_Δt (grey dashed box), p1 and p_{1+Δt} (purple dashed box), joined by grey arrows. The particles start as two clusters at the left and right edges. They move toward the center, merge, and then split into top and bottom clusters. The bold captions are "Wasserstein Lagrangian flow" and "Wasserstein Hamiltonian mechanics".
caption: Learning population mechanics with WLM: In (a), we illustrate the principle of least Wasserstein action (3): given observed marginals p0 and p1, the true interpolants form a minimal action curve in the space of densities, with respect to a population-level Lagrangian action. Alternative curves of densities have higher action and are drawn in red. Wasserstein least action induces Hamiltonian mechanics on the population, which we visualize in the state space for a population of interacting Boids in (b). Our method (WLM) learns these mechanics to interpolate and forecast unseen marginals (dashed grey and violet panels).
abstract: The population dynamics of molecules, cells, and organisms are governed by a number of unknown forces. In the last decade, population dynamics have predominantly been modeled with Wasserstein gradient flows. However, since gradient flows minimize free energy, they fail to capture important dynamical properties, such as periodicity. In this work, we propose a change in perspective by considering dynamics that minimize a population-level action under a damped Wasserstein Lagrangian. By deriving the corresponding Hamiltonian equations of motion, we formalize Wasserstein Lagrangian Mechanics, a structured class of second-order dynamics that encompasses classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and gradient flows. We then propose WLM as the first algorithm that learns these second-order dynamics from observed marginals, without specifying the Lagrangian. By directly learning the population mechanics, WLM can both forecast and interpolate unseen marginals, and outperforms existing gradient flow and flow matching methods across a wide range of dynamics, including vortex dynamics, embryonic development, and flocking.
